1. The model exhibits a severe upward bias when the 30-day forecast exceeds the current historical average by more than 5%, particularly during periods of low-to-moderate sentiment (0.00–0.20).
2. When sentiment history shows isolated spikes (e.g., 0.40) followed by silence, the model fails to capture the subsequent volatility and often predicts a smooth linear trend instead of mean-reverting behavior.
3. The model consistently overshoots true outcomes during high-volatility regimes; specifically, it predicts higher prices than realized when the true outcome drops below the 75th percentile of the historical range within the first 10 days.
4. There is a significant lag in detecting downward corrections; the model maintains an upward trajectory even after the true price has dropped 10–15% from its starting point, ignoring immediate negative momentum signals.
5. In high-price environments (above 90), the model's linear extrapolation fails to account for mean reversion, resulting in systematic overestimation compared to the volatile true outcomes which frequently dip below the forecasted path before recovering.
